<reason>Both sides argued competently and stayed on-topic, but CON built a tighter, more coherent path to victory. Its capture argument (aggressive enforcement falls on undercapitalized smallholders while conglomerates absorb or evade it) and leakage argument (demand migrates to weaker-oversight frontiers) were sustained across rounds and sharpened into a clean closing frame: certain, immediate costs to identifiable poor households versus an uncertain, unsized, capacity-dependent benefit. PRO's clever move—that CON's own "enforce existing rules" alternative concedes usable state capacity—was a good tu quoque, and PRO's distinction between "closing legal exceptions" and "mere enforcement" was a fair rejoinder, but PRO never recovered from its own admission in [B4.4] that leakage "must count against us" and cannot be sized; CON correctly converted that concession into a burden-of-proof win, arguing that a policy demanding certain sacrifice must show the offsetting benefit is real. PRO's rebuttals largely restated that displacement "doesn't establish" enough harm rather than substantively rebuilding the net-benefit case. CON's closing ("who should carry the risk of being wrong") crystallized the clash more decisively than PRO's closing, which mostly reasserted the externality framing without resolving the capacity/leakage doubts CON had raised.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>CON's Pressure Question on leakage burden-shifting, followed by PRO's answer conceding leakage "must count against us" without being able to size it, and CON's Rebuttal 2 turning that concession into an admission that the benefit side of PRO's case is unproven — this exchange was the most decisive turning point.</best_rebuttal>
